title: Ang 340–345: Kabir's letters and days
hook: Kabir's own alphabet, lunar days and weekdays
tomorrow: a city with no tax and no fear. who dreamed it up?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the weaver's questions: Kabir in Gauri, asking out loud what birth is supposed to prove. He isn't finished. Before Gauri closes, he picks up the alphabet itself.

It's past midnight. The cursor blinks. The toast is due Friday, and you've typed Welcome, everyone four times and deleted it four times. Every letter on the keyboard is right there, and none of them will say the thing. On ang 340 of the Guru Granth Sahib, a weaver sits down with the same problem and a far bigger subject. He knows the letters will fail him. He writes out the whole alphabet anyway. Why?
screen: `PAST MIDNIGHT. THE CURSOR BLINKS.` → `EVERY LETTER, AND NOTHING SAID.` → `SO WHY WRITE THEM ALL?`

segments.voice: From ang 340, Kabir takes the letters one at a time and hangs a line of teaching on each. The Granth calls it Bavan Akhri, the fifty-two letters, and Kabir names the number himself in its opening lines. In paraphrase: the three worlds are all described with these fifty-two letters; these letters will wear away; that other Word isn't among them. So the poem begins by admitting it can't do the job. Every letter after that is an arrow, not the target. A few lessons back we met Guru Arjan's fifty-two letters; this is the weaver's version, shorter and blunter. Then Kabir does the same with time. On ang 343, his Thiti walks through the days of the moon, and he says, in paraphrase: fifteen lunar days and seven weekdays, and the One has no near shore and no far one. Then the seven weekdays, one by one, each a reason to sing. Letters, days of the month, days of the week: the things we use to spell and measure everything. Kabir turns each one toward the One it can't hold. That's the answer to the blinking cursor. The words were never going to contain it. They point. And pointing is enough to begin.
screen: `FIFTY-TWO LETTERS, ONE BY ONE.` · `THESE LETTERS WILL WEAR AWAY.` · `MOON DAYS AND WEEKDAYS TOO.` · `THE WORDS POINT; THEY DON'T HOLD.` · then, large: `KABIR'S ALPHABET.`

segments.voice: Open ang 340 in a Gurbani app if one is near, and read the opening lines slowly, aloud or under your breath. Then, by hand, write one letter, any letter of any alphabet, on paper or with a fingertip on your palm. Rest with it for the sit: one small shape doing its best to point at something larger.
Ang 340. A page of the Guru Granth Sahib, where Kabir's fifty-two letters begin, near the end of Gauri.
For the road: Kabir's alphabet, every letter an arrow, none of them the target. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1485 COUNTS.` → `A WALK THROUGH THE GRANTH · 39 OF 180.` → `TOMORROW: A CITY WITH NO TAX AND NO FEAR. WHO DREAMED IT UP?`

Week two: the tent falls through (1492), Bebe misses her late husband while hanging the lights (1493), Maya learns Gurmukhi letters for the card (1494), the wedding, with Maya at her first gurdwara wedding and langar (1495, the unity arc), the empty house after (1496), Jasleen's thank-you card (1497), thank-you notes (1498).
